title: Solid Geometry
lines: Solid geometry on the CSCA is mostly formula work (areas and volumes), a few true-or-false statements about lines and planes, and coordinate calculations in 3-D. Draw a quick sketch and label every length you know.
## Prisms and pyramids
- Prism: two congruent parallel bases joined by parallelogram faces. Volume V = Sh (S = base area, h = height).
- Cuboid a × b × c: V = abc, surface area 2(ab + bc + ca), space diagonal √(a² + b² + c²). Cube of edge a: diagonal a√3.
- Pyramid: V = ⅓Sh. A regular pyramid has a regular-polygon base and its apex above the base's centre.
- Frustum (cut pyramid or cone): V = ⅓h(S + √(SS′) + S′), with S, S′ the two base areas.
- Surface area = sum of the areas of all faces.
> Example: A regular square pyramid has base edge 6 and height 4. Find its volume and lateral surface area.
> V = ⅓ · 36 · 4 = 48. Slant height of a face (apex to midpoint of a base edge) = √(4² + 3²) = 5. Each triangular face has area ½ · 6 · 5 = 15, so the lateral area is 60.
> Example: A cube has edge 2. Find the length of its space diagonal.
! Trap: the slant height of a face is not the height of the pyramid, and not the lateral edge. In the example the lateral edge is √(4² + (3√2)²) = √34.
! Trap: a pyramid's volume has the factor ⅓. A prism with the same base and height has three times the volume.
## Cylinders, cones and spheres
- Cylinder (radius r, height h): V = πr²h; lateral area 2πrh; total area 2πr² + 2πrh.
- Cone (radius r, height h, slant height l = √(r² + h²)): V = ⅓πr²h; lateral area πrl; total area πr² + πrl.
- Unrolled cone: a sector with radius l and arc length 2πr. Its central angle is 2πr/l (radians).
- Sphere (radius R): V = (4/3)πR³; surface area 4πR².
- Cross-section of a sphere at distance d from the centre: a circle of radius √(R² − d²).
> Example: A cone has radius 3 and height 4. Find its volume and lateral area.
> l = 5. V = ⅓π · 9 · 4 = 12π. Lateral area π · 3 · 5 = 15π.
> Example: The lateral surface of a cone unrolls into a semicircle of radius 4. Find the cone's base radius.
> Arc length = half of 2π·4 = 4π = 2πr, so r = 2.
> Example: A sphere's surface area is 36π. Find its volume.
> Example: A plane at distance 1 from the centre of a sphere of radius 2 cuts it. Find the area of the cross-section.
> r² = 4 − 1 = 3, area 3π.
! Scaling rule: if all lengths are multiplied by k, areas are multiplied by k² and volumes by k³. Doubling a sphere's radius multiplies its volume by 8.
## Inscribed and circumscribed spheres
- A cuboid's vertices lie on a sphere whose diameter is the space diagonal: 2R = √(a² + b² + c²).
- For a cube of edge a: circumscribed sphere R = (√3/2)a; inscribed sphere r = a/2; sphere touching all edges r = (√2/2)a.
- For a regular tetrahedron of edge a: height (√6/3)a, volume (√2/12)a³.
> Example: A cuboid 1 × 2 × 2 has all vertices on a sphere. Find the sphere's surface area.
! Trick: if three edges at one vertex are mutually perpendicular (for example PA, PB, PC in a "corner" tetrahedron), complete the cuboid. Its circumscribed sphere is the same.
## Lines and planes in space
- Two lines in space are parallel, intersecting, or skew (not parallel and not meeting, so not in one plane).
- Line parallel to plane: if a line outside a plane is parallel to some line in the plane, it is parallel to the plane.
- Plane parallel to plane: if two intersecting lines in one plane are each parallel to the other plane, the planes are parallel.
- If a plane meets two parallel planes, the two lines of intersection are parallel.
- Line perpendicular to plane: a line perpendicular to two intersecting lines in a plane is perpendicular to the plane. Then it is perpendicular to every line in that plane.
- Two lines perpendicular to the same plane are parallel.
- Planes perpendicular: if a plane contains a line perpendicular to another plane, the two planes are perpendicular.
- Three-perpendiculars idea: if PO ⊥ plane α and a line in α is perpendicular to the projection OA, it is perpendicular to PA as well.

> Example: Which is true? (i) Two lines parallel to the same plane are parallel. (ii) Two lines perpendicular to the same plane are parallel. (iii) Two planes perpendicular to the same plane are parallel.
> (i) false: they may intersect or be skew. (ii) true. (iii) false: two walls of a room are both perpendicular to the floor but meet in a corner. Answer: (ii) only.
! Trick: test space statements in a classroom or a cube. Floor, walls, edges and diagonals give counterexamples quickly.
! Trap: "perpendicular to two lines in the plane" is not enough if the two lines are parallel; they must intersect.
## 3-D rectangular coordinates
- A point is P(x, y, z). Points on the x-axis look like (a, 0, 0); points in the xOy plane look like (a, b, 0).
- Distance: |AB| = √((x₂ − x₁)² + (y₂ − y₁)² + (z₂ − z₁)²).
- Midpoint: ((x₁ + x₂)/2, (y₁ + y₂)/2, (z₁ + z₂)/2).
- Symmetric points of (x, y, z): about the origin (−x, −y, −z); about the xOy plane (x, y, −z); about the z-axis (−x, −y, z).
- Vectors in space work like plane vectors with a third coordinate: a·b = x₁x₂ + y₁y₂ + z₁z₂.
> Example: A(1, 2, −1) and B(3, 0, 1). Find |AB| and the midpoint.
> Example: Find the point symmetric to (2, −3, 4) about the xOy plane.
! Trap: reflecting about an axis keeps that axis's coordinate and changes the other two; reflecting about a plane changes only the coordinate not in the plane.
## Simple angles in solids
- Angle between skew lines: move one line parallel until they meet; the angle is in (0, π/2]. With vectors: cos θ = |a·b|/(|a||b|).
- Angle between a line and a plane: the angle between the line and its projection on the plane, in [0, π/2].
- Dihedral angle: the angle between two lines, one in each plane, both perpendicular to the common edge at the same point.
> Example: In the unit cube ABCD-A₁B₁C₁D₁ (A₁ above A, and so on), find the angle between the skew lines A₁B and AD₁.
> Example: In the same unit cube, find the angle between the diagonal AC₁ and the base ABCD.
> The projection of AC₁ on the base is AC = √2, and CC₁ = 1. tan θ = 1/√2 = √2/2, so sin θ = 1/√3 = √3/3.
! Trap: the angle between two lines is never obtuse. If the dot product is negative, take the absolute value.
! Trick: in a cube, the face diagonals A₁B, BC₁ and A₁C₁ form an equilateral triangle, so any two of them meet at 60°.
